explanations.answer: His eyes are too full of conceit
explanations.explanation: That's the reason David gives. The psalm says, "For his eyes are too full of conceit to detect or hate his own sin." (Psalm 36:2) He can't detect it, and he can't hate it either. I think when you're that full of yourself, spotting your own mistakes gets awfully hard.

David doesn't mention God's law or any lessons in this verse. The reason he gives is that the man's eyes are too full of conceit to detect or hate his own sin (Psalm 36:2). So the verse points to conceit. I think plenty of folks could hand him a book and he'd still be busy admiring his own reflection.

explanations.answer: His friends cover it up for him
explanations.explanation: Friends never show up in this verse. David says, "…his eyes are too full of conceit to detect or hate his own sin." (Psalm 36:2) The reason he gives is the man's own conceit. I think he's just too full of himself to look.

Oh, friend, no. David says the opposite. "The words of his mouth are wicked and deceitful…" (Psalm 36:3) You wouldn't trust this man to tell you the oven's hot, and I'd still check it with my own mustache.

That's right, baker. The psalm says, "The words of his mouth are wicked and deceitful; he has ceased to be wise and well-doing." (Psalm 36:3) Wicked and deceitful is how David describes the words of his mouth. David isn't being gentle here.
Yes, on his bed. David says, "Even on his bed he plots wickedness…" (Psalm 36:4) That's a place most of us go to rest, and he's still scheming. I think this man doesn't clock out.
The city gate isn't in this psalm. David says the man plots wickedness "Even on his bed…" (Psalm 36:4) The surprise is the bed. I think a bed is the last place you'd expect a plot.

The temple courts never come up in this psalm. David says the man plots wickedness "Even on his bed…" (Psalm 36:4) A BED! That's where most of us go to flop over and snore, and I think this man is in there cooking up a scheme instead. That's the surprising spot.

True, baker. David says, "he sets himself on a path that is not good…" (Psalm 36:4) Notice who does the setting: he sets himself on it. Nobody pushed him onto that path. The same verse adds that he fails to reject evil.

Not quite, friend. David says, "he sets himself on a path that is not good; he fails to reject evil." (Psalm 36:4) So David does say it, and the man is the one doing the setting. The same verse adds that he fails to reject evil.

That's it. David turns and says, "Your loving devotion, O LORD, reaches to the heavens…" (Psalm 36:5) He quits talking about the wicked man and starts talking straight to God. I love a turn like that, because it's like walking out of a messy kitchen into a warm one.

Not this time, baker. David says, "Your loving devotion, O LORD, reaches to the heavens, Your faithfulness to the clouds." (Psalm 36:5) That "Your" is aimed at the LORD. David is speaking right to Him.

David isn't turning to a crowd here. He says, "Your loving devotion, O LORD, reaches to the heavens…" (Psalm 36:5) The "You" is the LORD Himself. So David goes from describing the wicked man to speaking straight to God.

Right, the highest mountains. David says, "Your righteousness is like the highest mountains…" (Psalm 36:6) After reaching up to the sky, he plants his feet on the tallest ground there is. Big, solid and not going anywhere.

Cedars are tall, but they're not what David picks. He says, "Your righteousness is like the highest mountains…" (Psalm 36:6) Mountains are the picture, and he goes right to the highest ones. I'd have said "big tree" and called it a day.

A tower is strong, but David reaches for something else. "Your righteousness is like the highest mountains…" (Psalm 36:6) Nothing built by hands, just the highest mountains. That's a lot bigger than anything I could stamp.
True. David ends the verse with, "O LORD, You preserve man and beast." (Psalm 36:6) People and animals both. God's care covers the whole bunch.

Look again, friend. David says, "O LORD, You preserve man and beast." (Psalm 36:6) People and animals, both in the same breath, so the statement is true. And the beasts get named right alongside us, which makes me happy.

Yes, that's the picture. David says, "…the children of men take refuge in the shadow of Your wings!" (Psalm 36:7) A shadow like that is a place to tuck in close. I think anybody who's ever wanted somewhere safe to rest would know what that feels like.
A rock isn't the picture David uses here. He says people "…take refuge in the shadow of Your wings!" (Psalm 36:7) The picture is wings, and the shadow they cast.

Walls would make sense for a refuge, but that's not David's picture. He says, "…the children of men take refuge in the shadow of Your wings!" (Psalm 36:7) Wings, and the shadow they cast. Walls keep things out, while wings sound like they hold you close.
True, baker. David says, "They feast on the abundance of Your house…" (Psalm 36:8) The word is feast, and the word is abundance. Nobody's picking at crumbs there.
Check the verse, friend. David says, "They feast on the abundance of Your house…" (Psalm 36:8) That's the people taking refuge in God, and they're feasting. So it's true, and the table is full.
That's the one. David says, "For with You is the fountain of life…" (Psalm 36:9) Life itself, and it's with God. I think that's good news for everybody.
The spring of Gihon doesn't appear in this psalm. David says, "For with You is the fountain of life…" (Psalm 36:9) The fountain is with God, and he calls it the fountain of life.

The well of Bethlehem shows up in David's own story (2 Samuel 23:15), but not in this psalm. Here he says, "For with You is the fountain of life…" (Psalm 36:9) The fountain is with God, and it's all about life.

Yes, know. David prays, "Extend Your loving devotion to those who know You…" (Psalm 36:10) He's asking God to keep His loving devotion coming to the people who know Him. A prayer like that is a good one to borrow.

Not that one, baker. David says, "Extend Your loving devotion to those who know You…" (Psalm 36:10) The word is know. Forgetting isn't in the verse, and his prayer is for loving devotion to reach those who know God.

Not that one, friend. The verse says, "Extend Your loving devotion to those who know You…" (Psalm 36:10) The word is know, and that one little word is the whole difference. I once misread a recipe card by a single word, and trust me, the cookies told on me.

Right. David prays, "…nor the hand of the wicked drive me away." (Psalm 36:11) He doesn't want to be pushed out. I know a little about being pushed to the back of a drawer, so I get why that prayer matters.
A crown never comes up in this psalm. David prays, "…nor the hand of the wicked drive me away." (Psalm 36:11) That's what he asks God not to let happen. Losing a title isn't in the verse.

Nice guess for a psalm, but no. David prays, "…nor the hand of the wicked drive me away." (Psalm 36:11) What he asks is that the hand of the wicked not drive him away. His songs aren't mentioned in the verse.
Not this time, friend. David says, "There the evildoers lie fallen, thrown down and unable to rise." (Psalm 36:12) Unable to rise means they stay down. So the answer is False.

That's right. The psalm closes with, "There the evildoers lie fallen, thrown down and unable to rise." (Psalm 36:12) They're fallen and thrown down, and they can't get up. They don't bounce right back.
